messages.author: 8bbb9bd0a8e64bbb
messages.subject: Modeling non-linear relationships in Stan
parts:
I saw on the web an idea for modeling non-linear relationships that I'm playing around with in Stan but am finding it difficult to implement.  Probably, a huge part of this difficulty is knowing what to do once I've diagnosed a sampling problem.  The issue has been a large number of divergent transitions happening after warmup is complete.  I've tried adding stronger priors, increasing adapt_delta (as suggested in the information message).  Despite setting adapt_delta to several higher values (and having to increase max_treedepth) I still get divergent transitions.  Obviously, there's either a) something wrong with my code, or b) this is just a really difficult posterior to sample from.  Does anyone have any thoughts—any help would be greatly appreciated?  Code and sessionInfo() below.

sessionInfo:

R version 3.2.3 (2015-12-10)
Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin13.4.0 (64-bit)
Running under: OS X 10.10.5 (Yosemite)

locale:
[1] en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/C/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8

attached base packages:
[1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base     

other attached packages:
[1] rstan_2.9.0-3 ggplot2_2.0.0

loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
 [1] colorspace_1.2-6 scales_0.3.0     plyr_1.8.3       parallel_3.2.3   tools_3.2.3     
 [6] inline_0.3.14    gtable_0.1.2     gridExtra_2.0.0  Rcpp_0.12.1      codetools_0.2-14
[11] grid_3.2.3       munsell_0.4.2    stats4_3.2.3  

Code:

library("rstan")
set.seed(1313)

x = seq(-1,1,length=1000)
y = 0.5 + x - x^2 + rnorm(1000)

dat = list(x=as.vector(scale(x)), y=as.vector(scale(y)))
dat = c(n=length(dat$x), dat)

mods = "
data{
  int n;
  real x[n];
  real y[n];
}

parameters{
  vector[n-1] delta_unif;
  real<lower=0> delta_sd;
  real intercept;
  real<lower=0> obs_sd;
}

transformed parameters{
  vector[n] mu;
  vector[n-1] delta;

  delta[1] <- 0.00267 * delta_unif[1];

  for(i in 2:(n-1))
    delta[i] <- delta[i-1] + delta_sd * delta_unif[i];

  mu[1] <- intercept;

  for(i in 2:n)
    mu[i] <- mu[i-1] + delta[i-1];
}

model{
  intercept ~ normal(0,4);
  obs_sd ~ student_t(7,0,8);
  delta_sd ~ normal(0,.000889);
  delta_unif ~ normal(0,1);
  y ~ normal(mu,obs_sd);
}
"

mod.stan = stan(model_code = mods, data=dat, chains=4, cores=2, seed=9838)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling non-linear relationships in Stan
parts:
You don't seem to use x in the program.

I think what you're doing works out to this
latent time series in mu:

mu[1] ~ normal(0, 4);
for (n in 2:N)
mu[n] ~ normal(mu[n - 1], sigma_mu);

with additional measurement error for the data y:

y ~ normal(mu, sigma_y);

(I renamed your scale terms to follow our conventions).

That can be hard to fit. What's happening to the
estimates of obs_sd and delta_sd? Is one of them
going to zero?

- Bob

messages.author: 8bbb9bd0a8e64bbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling non-linear relationships in Stan
parts: Hi, Bob, thanks for the response!

On Sunday, February 21, 2016 at 1:05:56 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
You don't seem to use x in the program.

Right, in this toy example x is really just a grid and so is not really used directly for anything other than generating y.  In a real example multiple observations might come at each unique value of x (and this program would have to be revised slightly).  Then x would be an integer identifying which mu[] each observation comes from (and hence wouldn't be scaled as I have done!).

I think what you're doing works out to this
latent time series in mu:

  mu[1] ~ normal(0, 4);
  for (n in 2:N)
    mu[n] ~ normal(mu[n - 1], sigma_mu);

with additional measurement error for the data y:

 y ~ normal(mu, sigma_y);

(I renamed your scale terms to follow our conventions).

Right, this general code looks very similar to how I started out, although my thought was to use delta_sd to control the evolution of the deltas (derivatives), rather than directly the mu's themselves (perhaps similar to penalising the size of the second derivative?  Not 100% sure.).  I tried to rephrase things in terms of the "Matt trick" from the manual in hopes of improving things which didn't really help much.

That can be hard to fit.  What's happening to the
estimates of obs_sd and delta_sd?  Is one of them
going to zero?

Posterior samples of obs_sd are in the range of .7–.8-ish, but delta_sd's are very small (on the order of 1e-5, I think).  My intuition (maybe wrong) is that while the values of function do change overall (and is not linear), changes between successive grid points are going to be very small, especially on a tight grid.  Maybe that's causing a problem?

It sounds like fitting this type of model in Stan might not be realistic.

Thanks for your help!

> Right, in this toy example x is really just a grid and so is not really used directly for anything other than generating y. In a real example multiple observations might come at each unique value of x (and this program would have to be revised slightly). Then x would be an integer identifying which mu[] each observation comes from (and hence wouldn't be scaled as I have done!).

Afraid I didn't understand that, but it looks like it's
not relevant for the case at hand (at least not yet).

>
> I think what you're doing works out to this
> latent time series in mu:
>
> mu[1] ~ normal(0, 4);
> for (n in 2:N)
> mu[n] ~ normal(mu[n - 1], sigma_mu);
>
> with additional measurement error for the data y:
>
> y ~ normal(mu, sigma_y);
>
> (I renamed your scale terms to follow our conventions).
>
> Right, this general code looks very similar to how I started out, although my thought was to use delta_sd to control the evolution of the deltas (derivatives), rather than directly the mu's themselves (perhaps similar to penalising the size of the second derivative? Not 100% sure.).

They're exactly the same. Because of the form of the
normal log density, if you do this:

for (n in 2:N) {
delta <- mu[n] - mu[n - 1];
delta ~ normal(0, sigma_mu);
}

you get exactly the same density as if you do this:

The latter's just the typical way of writing a time series.

It's modeling the difference from the previous value either way.

> I tried to rephrase things in terms of the "Matt trick" from the manual in hopes of improving things which didn't really help much.
>
>
> That can be hard to fit. What's happening to the
> estimates of obs_sd and delta_sd? Is one of them
> going to zero?
>
> Posterior samples of obs_sd are in the range of .7–.8-ish, but delta_sd's are very small (on the order of 1e-5, I think). My intuition (maybe wrong) is that while the values of function do change overall (and is not linear), changes between successive grid points are going to be very small, especially on a tight grid. Maybe that's causing a problem?
>
> It sounds like fitting this type of model in Stan might not be realistic.

I'm not surprised that's what happens. Just look at what happens
to the density as delta_sd -> 0 and all the mu approach the same value.
So it's not just Stan, it's that your model's not really well
identified for the data you have. Stan's very good at identifying these
pathologies in models and data.

With very little data, your prior's going to keep delta_sd very low.
What happens if you relax that prior?

Basically, I'd try to simulate data according to the model and see if
you can recover it. But with no predictors or anything else to grab
onto, there may just not be enough info to keep delta_sd from degenerating.

- Bob
